slides.title: From molecule to medicine
bullets: How a new drug goes from the lab to the pharmacy
Discovery, testing, approval and safety monitoring
slides.notes: Welcome. Today we walk through how a new medicine is developed, from the first idea in the lab to a product patients can use. You can say next, go back, jump to any slide, or ask me a question at any time.

slides.title: Drug discovery
bullets: Pick a disease target, such as a protein or gene
Screen thousands of compounds for activity
Optimise the best hits into a lead candidate
slides.notes: Discovery starts with a biological target linked to a disease. Scientists screen large libraries of compounds to find ones that act on that target, then chemists refine the most promising hits to improve potency, selectivity and safety. Only a handful of candidates move forward.

slides.title: Preclinical testing
bullets: Lab and animal studies before any human dosing
Check toxicity, dosing range and how the body handles the drug
Run under Good Laboratory Practice (GLP)
slides.notes: Before a drug can be given to people, it is tested in cells and animals. These studies look at toxicity, a safe starting dose, and pharmacokinetics, meaning how the drug is absorbed, distributed, metabolised and excreted. The results support an application to start human trials, such as an Investigational New Drug application in the United States.

slides.title: Clinical trials
bullets: Phase 1: safety and dosing in a small group
Phase 2: early effectiveness and side effects in patients
Phase 3: large trials confirming benefit against standard care
slides.notes: Clinical development runs in phases. Phase 1 usually involves a small number of healthy volunteers or patients and focuses on safety and dose. Phase 2 tests whether the drug works in patients with the condition. Phase 3 enrols much larger groups to confirm effectiveness and monitor side effects. Most candidates that enter clinical trials do not reach approval, and the whole journey often takes ten years or more.

slides.title: Regulatory approval
bullets: Submit all data to regulators: NDA or BLA to the US FDA, MAA to the EMA
Regulators review safety, efficacy and manufacturing quality
Approval comes with an agreed label for doctors and patients
slides.notes: Once Phase 3 is complete, the company submits a full dossier to regulators. In the United States that is a New Drug Application or Biologics License Application to the FDA. In Europe it is a Marketing Authorisation Application to the European Medicines Agency, and in India the regulator is the CDSCO. Reviewers check the benefit-risk balance and whether the drug can be manufactured consistently.

slides.title: Manufacturing and quality
bullets: Produced under Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP)
Every batch tested for identity, purity and strength
Sites are inspected by regulators
slides.notes: Approved medicines must be made under Good Manufacturing Practice. That means controlled processes, validated equipment, trained staff and full documentation. Each batch is tested before release, and regulators inspect manufacturing sites to make sure standards are maintained.

slides.title: Pharmacovigilance
bullets: Safety monitoring continues after launch
Doctors and patients report adverse events
Labels can be updated, or a drug withdrawn, if new risks appear
slides.notes: Clinical trials cannot detect every rare side effect, so monitoring continues once the drug is on the market. This is called pharmacovigilance. Adverse event reports from doctors, patients and studies are collected and analysed, and companies may run Phase 4 studies. If new risks emerge, regulators can require label changes or, in serious cases, withdraw the product.

slides.title: Questions
bullets: Ask about any stage of drug development
Say 'start over' to go back to the beginning
slides.notes: That brings us to the end of the journey from molecule to medicine. I'm happy to answer questions about discovery, trials, approval, manufacturing or safety monitoring.
